channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: AI measurements of heart scans more strongly linked to patient survival than clinician measurements
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) measurements of heart function from MRI scans are more strongly linked to how long patients live after their scan than measurements made by clinicians, suggesting that AI could provide a useful first-line approach to measuring heart function. This is according to research led by City St George's, University of London and University College London, and published in The Lancet Digital Health.

item.title: Natural plant compound may help overcome cancer drug resistance
item.description: A natural plant compound may help overcome a built-in defense that allows many cancers to resist a class of drugs designed to restore normal gene activity, according to a study by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center.

item.title: A surge in brain connections fine-tunes visual responses within days of eyes opening, study finds
item.description: Our brain's wiring is shaped both by genes and what we experience, and the visual system is a great model for studying how the two work together. Before the eyes ever open, genetic programs lay down a first draft of the brain's visual circuits. But once they open, experience takes over, with visual information refining the initial draft.

item.title: Reducing hallucinations in schizophrenia with focused ultrasound: First-in-human clinical trial begins
item.description: Auditory hallucinations—or hearing voices that others do not hear—affect more than 70% of people with schizophrenia. Despite treatment with antipsychotic medications, approximately 40% continue to experience persistent hallucinations. For these patients, new treatment approaches are urgently needed.

item.title: No neuralyzer needed: The molecular pathways and circuit that trigger forgetting in C. elegans
item.description: In the 1997 film "Men in Black," one of the prominent pieces of alien technology the main characters use in their work to police extraterrestrial activity on Earth was the neuralyzer. This flashy handheld device would erase the witnesses' memories of their close encounter. For as long as human inquiry has existed, people have tried to understand how and why we remember and forget. As we have begun to understand how the brain works, researchers have slowly uncovered the biological mechanisms underlying memory.

item.title: A single protein that helps drive responses to touch, temperature, pain and itch could offer a new drug target
item.description: A light brush, a hot surface and an irritating itch all activate different sensory pathways, yet researchers have determined that, in mice, these otherwise distinct responses share a molecular helper. A team led by Bailong Xiao at Tsinghua University found that removing the protein CRELD1 weakened the animals' reactions to touch, heat, cold, painful pressure and itch. But how can one protein influence so many different sensations?

item.title: How an innate immune protein can control cholesterol, tumor growth and response to cancer therapy
item.description: Scientists at the University of North Carolina Lineberger Comprehensive Cancer Center have discovered an unexpected role for a key innate immune protein, revealing how it helps regulate cholesterol levels inside cells and influences tumor growth and treatment response. The findings shed new light on how cancer cells rewire their metabolism—and point to potential new strategies for therapy.

item.title: Inpatient rehab, nursing facility or home? How to choose the right rehab after a hospital stay
item.description: A broken hip, a stroke or major surgery can leave you or someone you love needing weeks of therapy to walk, dress or speak again.

item.title: The surprising science of what pain is and why it hurts
item.description: When you step into an ice-cold lake, it would be nice if your body warned you about possible harm with a polite message: "Your feet may be at risk. Would you kindly consider stepping out?"

item.title: Vitamin C during pregnancy supports early brain development, study finds
item.description: New research from Oregon Health & Science University shows that additional vitamin C intake during pregnancy can be an effective, low-cost and accessible intervention to promote infant emotional well-being.

item.title: Cervical cancer cases and deaths forecast to rise
item.description: Global cervical cancer cases and deaths could rise by 20.2% and 39.3%, respectively, by 2050, according to a modeling study published in Nature Medicine. The findings suggest that the burden of cervical cancer will remain unevenly distributed, with the highest incidence and mortality rates in sub-Saharan Africa.

item.title: Medicare spending rises after private equity buys hospices
item.description: A study of for-profit hospices acquired by private equity firms found that Medicare spending rose by 5.9% per hospice stay after acquisition, compared with similar for-profit hospices that weren't acquired. The increase was driven mainly by longer stays, with the average length of stay rising by 6.3 days. This was likely related to shifts toward patients who use less daily care, including a significant increase in the share of patients with dementia, consistent with a larger share of patients discharged from hospice alive.

item.title: Hereditary lung and liver disease successfully treated for the first time using gene correction
item.description: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATM) is a congenital metabolic disorder. It is caused by a genetic defect, which results in the protective protein alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) being produced incorrectly. This deficiency primarily damages the lungs and the liver, where it can lead to serious conditions such as pulmonary emphysema, liver fibrosis or cirrhosis. In particularly severe cases, an organ transplant is the last resort. There is as yet no curative treatment.

item.title: Targeting hormone receptors reduces lupus-related kidney damage in mice
item.description: Researchers at the University of California, Riverside, and City of Hope have identified a new strategy for treating systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), or lupus, an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks healthy tissues. By targeting an imbalance in receptors for the hormone prolactin in disease-causing immune cells, the team reduced inflammatory molecules and harmful immune cells while preserving their normal counterparts.

item.title: Study shows AI may improve patient discharge summaries
item.description: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) could help physicians prepare hospital patient discharge summaries more efficiently and with greater accuracy and completeness. This is the conclusion of a Stony Brook University study published online in npj Digital Medicine.

item.title: Ebola outbreak kills more than 5,300 people: Africa CDC
item.description: Africa's latest Ebola outbreak has killed more than 5,300 people, the vast majority of them in the Democratic Republic of Congo, according to the continent's top health agency.

item.title: ASN: Fruits and vegetables improve outcomes in stage 3 chronic kidney disease
item.description: For patients with stage 3 chronic kidney disease (CKD), receiving fruits and vegetables (F&V) is associated with better clinical outcomes than standard treatment with sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃ [HCO₃]) or usual care, according to a study presented at Kidney Week, the annual meeting of the American Society of Nephrology, held from Oct. 21 to 25 in Denver.

item.title: Study provides reassuring news for women using medications to treat opioid use disorder during pregnancy
item.description: Pregnant patients receiving medication to treat opioid use disorder should not reduce their medication dose out of fear that it will worsen withdrawal symptoms in their newborns, according to a new study led by researchers at the University of Maryland School of Medicine (UMSOM).

item.title: How the immune system gets better at detecting pathogens
item.description: B cells, a type of white blood cell, protect our bodies by producing antibodies that recognize and bind to invaders like bacteria and viruses. After an infection, B cells undergo rapid mutations in the genes that encode antibodies. These mutations—known as somatic hypermutations—allow B cells to produce antibodies tailor-made to recognize the foreign pathogens they just encountered, making them more efficient at defense.

item.title: Postop morbidity lower with laparoscopic versus open resection of colorectal liver metastases
item.description: For patients with colorectal liver metastases (CRLM), laparoscopic liver resection (LLR) is associated with lower postoperative morbidity than open liver resection (OLR), with similar long-term oncologic outcomes, according to a study published online Oct. 27 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

item.title: Engineers address key hurdle for exhaled breath diagnostics
item.description: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a chronic condition that causes increasing difficulty in breathing as it progresses, is the third leading cause of death worldwide. The clinical diagnosis and monitoring of COPD and other pulmonary diseases can be taxing, often requiring blood testing, which can be uncomfortable for patients, or costly imaging procedures, such as CT scans. Additionally, COPD flare-ups can occur unexpectedly and progress rapidly, significantly increasing the risk of death.

item.title: Are there better ways to protect athletes from blows to the head? Researchers test student football players
item.description: Getting concussed is usually obvious: there's dizziness, headache and confusion. The symptoms appear after a blow to the head or body and temporarily disrupt brain function.

item.title: 'Heart-in-a-dish' paves way for personalized treatment for heart failure
item.description: McGill researchers have developed a new way to study why the same heart failure treatment can help some patients recover while others continue to get worse.

item.title: Ensuring health equity with the use of AI
item.description: Only 13% of articles examined in a review of artificial intelligence (AI) and health equity explicitly defined health equity—a gap that could leave AI-driven approaches benefiting the most advantaged groups. That's a key finding from a review led by Caroline R. Efird of Georgetown University and colleagues. The research was published Oct. 8, 2026, in Health Affairs Scholar.

item.title: US approves cheap generic of breakthrough HIV shot for poorer countries
item.description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Monday approved a low-cost version of a twice-yearly HIV prevention shot, bringing the breakthrough drug closer to market in low-income countries.

item.title: RNA-protein interactions reveal new coronavirus drug targets
item.description: A study led by researchers at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine and University of California, Riverside (UCR) School of Medicine has identified new targets for antiviral drugs against coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. These new targets could help scientists discover treatments that are less vulnerable to the rapid evolution of these viruses.

item.title: Surgery offers best survival for early-stage lung cancer, study finds
item.description: Surgery should remain the primary treatment for people with early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who are suitable for either surgery or a highly targeted form of radiotherapy, a new study from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) suggests.

item.title: Extreme heat may raise suicide risk by disrupting sleep and emotional regulation, study finds
item.description: In a study conducted by the World Bank and Georgetown University, scientists, including lead author Syed Shabab Wahid, DrPH, are investigating how climate change–induced heat exposure is an emerging public health concern with potential mental health consequences.

item.title: Researchers identify strategy to make pediatric bone cancers more vulnerable to immunotherapy
item.description: Ewing sarcoma is a rare and debilitating type of bone cancer affecting young adults and children. Despite intensive treatment with chemotherapy, surgery and radiation, many children do not overcome the disease.

item.title: Exploring sex differences in how the brain adapts to overeating
item.description: Overeating alters neural pathways involved in feeding and metabolism, but how fast do these adaptive changes occur? And do these adaptations occur similarly in males and females?
